name: Tech-Right
overview: The Tech-Right's program is a nationalist version of the techno-optimism Andreessen set out in 2023: growth and technology make a nation strong, and stagnation is the real danger. Applied to the state, it means winning the AI race against China by letting labs ship without pre-release review and overriding fifty state rulebooks; building the power plants and data centers AI needs; rebuilding the arsenal with software-first firms such as Palantir and Anduril rather than the old primes; putting the dollar on crypto rails; and keeping doors open to engineers. Its best case is that America's edge over China is speed, and every rule is a gift to Beijing.

Each plank is also a portfolio. a16z raised about $15B in January, $1.176B of it for 'American Dynamism' (Anduril, Shield AI, Saronic, Castelion), and Saudi Arabia's Sanabil lists it as a holding (TechCrunch, Jan 9). Founders Fund, Thiel's firm, led Anduril's 2025 round with $1B; Thiel chairs Palantir, whose government revenue rose with the war; Sacks's Craft has 400+ AI-linked investments under ethics waivers; SpaceX takes about a fifth of its revenue from government. The political money is large: Musk gave about $446M and a16z and its founders $116M in the 2026 midterms (NYT via Axios, Nov 2). Its people write policy (Kratsios, Krishnan, Kupor) and its founders call the president directly (May 21).

Acts depart from the program where the portfolio and the nation diverge. 'Beat China' sits beside lobbying for H200 sales to China and license-free chips for the UAE (Jul 10), with Gulf funds (MGX, Qatar's fund) holding stakes in the same labs. 'Rebuild the arsenal' means Palantir's Maven use doubled in the Iran war while Thiel calls the war a mistake (Oct 12): the strategist objects, the shareholder collects. Musk capped Starshield speeds that Ukraine's drones need (Oct 13-14, disputed) and Trump reportedly had to call him to lift it. On skilled visas the faction stays quiet while Vance, whom its patrons made, suspended PERM filings (Oct 8).

Precedent: the Cold War military-industrial-academic alliance, when the state funded the labs and firms that built American supremacy. It breaks on who holds control: then the Pentagon set the agenda and owned the risk; now the vendors help write the rules (Sacks, Kratsios), fund the campaigns and count the state as a main customer, with Gulf capital in the cap tables (my reading).

November 9 review: Nvidia’s independent board inquiry creates new scrutiny of the company’s leadership and national-security exposure. My reading: commercial advocates may face stronger demands for answers from officials seeking tighter chip controls. The board’s support for Jensen Huang and its statement that it has no reason to believe secrets were compromised leave the outcome open; no new export restriction or unified faction position is established.

paras: Position.

No binding pre-release review; federal preemption of state laws; chip sales; open weights. The May 21 order was pulled (reported), though Trump signed the narrower Jun 2 order. Sep 29: Cruz blocked the 45-day review bill; the AI accord was signed.

Why the faction does it. Speed against China is the argument; the portfolios and funders gain from each plank (documented fit): a16z's $50M to Leading the Future, Brockman's $25M, Nvidia's H200 lobbying.
Who and why.
Sacks. Posture: rules hand the race to Beijing. Interest: Craft's 400+ AI bets and BitGo stake under broad waivers (Kathleen Clark: a 'sham', a 'pardon in advance').
Andreessen. Posture: techno-optimism. Interest: a16z's AI and defense portfolio and its $116M in the midterms.
Thiel. Posture: the West stagnates without technology. Interest: Palantir's state contracts and Founders Fund's defense bets.
Huang. Posture: American chips everywhere. Interest: H200 sales are Nvidia revenue; the $25M pledge buys access (my reading).
Kratsios, Krishnan, Kupor write the policy; Krishnan and Kupor came from a16z. No personal stake shown.
Say versus do. 'Beat China' while lobbying to sell China H200s, and Gulf funds in the same labs (my reading).

Stance audit. The ledger groups preemption, less review, and chip sales under one agenda. Identify the actors behind each ask. Industry spending and Nvidia lobbying establish different forms of support. a16z, Brockman, Founders Fund and Nvidia have different political or portfolio stakes. Export revenue and strategic limits on China can diverge. Split the planks before judging consistency. Campaign support and financial exposure alone leave policy influence unresolved.

paras: Position.
Dec 24, 2024: Musk vowed “war” for H-1B, citing an engineer shortage. He later softened to “broken.”
He has been silent on the fee and the PERM suspensions since.
Why the faction does it. A skilled-visa pipeline serves tech employers, but a public fight is costly for those who depend on the government.
Who and why.

Musk Motives: (1) Personal: he entered the US on an H-1B, by his own statement. (2) Business: his companies hire engineers who need visas, so a fee or a suspension raises his costs (my reading; headcount not sourced). (3) Exposure: SpaceX's government revenue and a Trump who has already threatened his companies explain the silence. The loud promise in Dec 2024 produced no act.
Kupor Motives: Background in venture capital, where skilled visas are the talent supply (background). No personal stake shown.
Vance acted against the faction on Oct 8 (see Vance Lane); the faction's donors have not publicly fought him.
